title: Rates, Units & Proportional Reasoning
coreInsight: A rate is a ratio connecting quantities with different units, and the units themselves reveal how the quantities relate.
targetLearnerRealization: The word 'per' connects two different units, and dimensional meaning often tells us whether to multiply or divide.
learningObjectives: Normalize a rate to an amount per one unit.
Use units to decide whether to multiply or divide.
Distinguish a rate from a total amount.
Recognize when a fixed extra amount prevents direct proportionality.

continuity.openingCallback: Turn a scaled ratio into a per-one quantity while keeping both units visible.
closingSeeds: A constant rate can be shown as a constant steepness on a graph.
Unit tracking can check multi-step calculations beyond rate problems.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Units can be ignored once numbers are written down.
Rate and total amount are the same kind of quantity.
Every rate problem is direct proportion.
The word per can be treated as decoration rather than division.

beats.purpose: Isolate normalization to one unit with visible dollar and ticket units.
beats.expectedRealization: Twelve dollars for three tickets compresses to four dollars per one ticket.
beats.transitionIn: The cyclist's 36 miles in 3 hours became 12 miles in 1 hour. Use the same batch-shrinking move with different units.
beats.prompt: Three identical tickets cost $12 altogether. What is the cost per ticket?

visual.ariaLabel: Three identical tickets sharing a total cost of twelve dollars

response.feedback: Share the total dollars equally among the three tickets.

beats.incorrectFeedback: The question asks for one ticket, so divide the total cost by the number of tickets.

steps.title: Normalize the batch
steps.body: Divide both quantities by 3: $12 for 3 tickets becomes $4 for 1 ticket.

steps.title: Keep the unit
steps.body: The result is not merely 4. It is 4 dollars per ticket.

resolution.takeaway: Per one comes from dividing by the number of units.

beats.purpose: Scale a unit rate back to a total and distinguish the two kinds of quantities.
beats.expectedRealization: A total cost combines dollars per ticket with a number of tickets.
beats.transitionIn: The batch is compressed to $4 per ticket. Now rebuild a larger purchase.
beats.prompt: At $4 per ticket, what is the total cost of 7 tickets?

response.feedback: Combine 4 dollars for each of 7 tickets.

beats.incorrectFeedback: The rate gives dollars for one ticket; repeat that amount seven times.

steps.title: Combine the units
steps.body: Multiplying dollars per ticket by tickets leaves dollars.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.body: $4/ticket × 7 tickets = $28. The rate is $4 per ticket; the total is $28.

resolution.takeaway: Rate × number of units = total amount.

beats.purpose: Use dimensional meaning to select division in an inverse-looking time question.
beats.expectedRealization: Dividing distance by distance per hour leaves hours.
beats.transitionIn: Units canceled tickets in the total-cost calculation. Let them choose an operation in a travel calculation.
beats.prompt: A train travels 180 miles at 60 miles per hour. Which calculation has the unit hours and answers how long the trip takes?
beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Miles divided by miles per hour leaves hours.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Choose the operation whose unit cancellation leaves the requested unit, hours.

steps.title: Write the units as a fraction
Divide
steps.body: 180 miles ÷ (60 miles/hour) = 180 miles × (1 hour/60 miles) = 3 hours. Miles cancel, leaving hours.

resolution.takeaway: Let the requested unit guide the operation.

beats.purpose: Show that a rate context can involve inverse rather than direct proportional change.
beats.expectedRealization: For a fixed distance, increasing speed decreases time.
beats.transitionIn: The trip time came from distance divided by speed. Hold the distance fixed and change the speed.
beats.prompt: For the same 180-mile trip, what happens to travel time if speed doubles from 60 to 120 miles per hour?
beats.correctFeedback: Right. With distance fixed, twice the speed takes half the time.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute 180 miles ÷ 120 miles per hour and compare with 3 hours.

steps.body: 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5 hours. Speed and time do not scale together here because their product must remain the fixed distance, 180 miles.

resolution.takeaway: A rate setting is not automatically direct proportion between every pair of quantities.

beats.purpose: Name rate and unit rate after learners have normalized, rebuilt, and canceled units.
beats.expectedRealization: A rate is a ratio with unlike units, and per signals division.
beats.transitionIn: Tickets, dollars, miles, and hours followed the same unit logic.
beats.name: Rate and unit rate
beats.conciseDefinition: A rate compares quantities with different units. A unit rate expresses the first quantity per one unit of the second quantity.
beats.formalization: amount per unit = amount ÷ number of units
beats.memoryHook: Per means divide; units tell the story.

beats.purpose: Revisit an estimated distance through the new lens of dimensional meaning and a two-step unit chain.
beats.expectedRealization: Seconds combine with feet per second to make feet, which then convert to miles.
beats.transitionIn: You have already seen that this storm's distance is about two miles. This time, make every operation earn the unit it produces.
beats.whyNow: After a clean unit-rate model, the lightning problem rewards tracking feet per second, seconds, feet, and miles rather than recalling a formula.
beats.entryBridge: Predict the answer unit, then keep it attached to every intermediate quantity.
beats.exitBridge: The unit chain both produced the answer and checked the operations.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Unit-labeled quantities that combine and convert in sequence.
learnerPrompts: Before advancing, name the unit the question requests.
At the distance step, explain why seconds × feet/second leaves feet.
At the conversion step, explain why dividing feet by feet/mile leaves miles.
At the final step, round 2.06 to the nearest allowed half-mile.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The unit chain produces about 2.06 miles, which rounds to 2 miles.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First multiply the speed by elapsed seconds to get feet; then divide by feet per mile to get miles.

steps.title: Use the requested precision
steps.body: 2.06 is closer to 2 than to 2.5, so the answer is C.

resolution.takeaway: A correct calculation should produce the requested unit.

beats.purpose: Repair the assumption that any situation mentioning a per-unit rate is directly proportional overall.
beats.expectedRealization: A fixed starting amount prevents the total from being a scaled copy of the variable part.
beats.transitionIn: The storm started from zero distance at zero seconds. Add a starting fee and test whether totals still scale directly.
beats.prompt: A rental costs a fixed $10 fee plus $4 per hour. Two hours cost $18. Does four hours cost twice as much, $36?

options.text: Yes, because every rate problem is proportional.
No; four hours cost $16 with no fee.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Only the hourly part doubles; the fixed fee is charged once.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Separate the one-time $10 from the $4 repeated for each hour.

steps.title: Separate fixed and variable parts
steps.body: At two hours the cost is $10 + $8 = $18. At four hours it is $10 + $16 = $26.

steps.title: Test proportionality
steps.body: Doubling hours does not double the total because the $10 fee does not scale.

resolution.takeaway: A per-unit component does not make an entire relationship proportional when a fixed amount is present.

beats.purpose: Independently combine normalization and inverse unit reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: A unit rate can be found first and then used to divide a target amount by output per minute.
beats.transitionIn: Use the unit logic without a prepared animation.
beats.prompt: A printer produces 45 pages in 3 minutes at a constant rate. How many minutes does it need to print 150 pages?

response.feedback: First find pages per minute, then choose the operation that leaves minutes.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The printer makes 15 pages per minute, and 150 pages ÷ 15 pages/minute = 10 minutes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide 45 pages by 3 minutes, then use the resulting pages-per-minute rate with 150 pages.

steps.title: Find time
steps.body: 150 pages ÷ 15 pages/minute = 10 minutes. Pages cancel, leaving minutes.

resolution.takeaway: Normalize, follow the units, and check by reversing the operation.

beats.purpose: Consolidate rate meaning, unit tracking, and proportionality conditions.
beats.expectedRealization: Units are structural evidence for both operations and interpretation.
beats.transitionIn: Tickets, travel, thunder, rentals, and printing all become clearer when units stay attached.
beats.prompt: Select every statement that belongs in reliable rate reasoning.

options.text: Treat “per” as division between named units.
Check that the calculation produces the requested unit.
Treat a rate and a total as the same kind of quantity.
Check for fixed amounts before assuming direct proportion.
Erase units before choosing an operation.

response.feedback: Use units as evidence, and test whether the entire relationship truly scales from zero.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Units guide the operation, and fixed terms warn that direct scaling may fail.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep statements that preserve units and test proportionality; discard those that erase meaning.

steps.title: Read
steps.body: Name both quantities and interpret per as division.

steps.title: Operate
steps.body: Multiply or divide so unwanted units cancel and the requested unit remains.

steps.title: Question
steps.body: A constant rate produces direct proportion only when no fixed starting amount changes the total.

resolution.takeaway: Units are part of the mathematics, not decoration.

notes: The opening isolates unit-rate meaning before the approved storm problem combines rate, time, conversion, and estimation.
The storm is revisited from F1 through a substantively new unit-cancellation lens rather than as repeated estimation practice.
The lesson remains draft pending human pedagogical review.
